papers.abstract: This study highlights the potential of using comic-based digital storytelling as an instructional strategy for digital safety education. Guided by the multimodal literacy theory, the study employs character analysis and biterm topic modeling to identify prevalent themes within the curated Pixton comics of 20 students. The study revealed digital footprint, netiquette, and privacy as key themes in student's comics. Comic characters represented students' self-inserts and revealed expressions of their understanding of the topics.

papers.title: A Case of Middle Schoolers Reasoning with Multiple Models in Science Learning: Quantitative, Qualitative, or Both?
papers.authors: Ayça K. Fackler, Laura A. Zangori, Swarna Mahapatra, Zhen Xu, Troy D. Sadler
papers.modelling_usage: **Statistical, Machine Learning & Quantitative Modeling**: Applies quantitative, statistical, or machine learning models (e.g., SEM, multilevel analysis, Markov, or network modeling) to examine learning processes and empirical outcomes. Evidence: "Therefore, this case study examined how middle school students shift back and forth between qualitative and quantitative reasoning through mechanistic and computational models to explain ..."
papers.abstract: Most attention on model-based reasoning only explores how students reason either qualitatively or quantitatively. Opportunities to reason about a phenomenon using qualitative models and quantitative modeling have rarely been explored. Yet, scientists require fluid movement between these reasoning structures using models that are qualitative and quantitative. Therefore, this case study examined how middle school students shift back and forth between qualitative and quantitative reasoning through mechanistic and computational models to explain how respiratory diseases spread.

papers.title: A Framework to Integrate Computational Modeling Practices with Three-dimensional NGSS Learning
papers.authors: Aditi Wagh, Daniel Wendel, Emma Anderson, Ilana Schoenfeld
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Computational modeling (CM) supports scientific and computational practices."
papers.abstract: Computational modeling (CM) supports scientific and computational practices. Little work has examined how CM practices align with the scientific and engineering practices (SEPs) in the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). This poster presents a conceptual framework to align five CM practices with SEPs. This framework is being used to develop CM NGSS-aligned curriculum for high school science classrooms in a district. We provide one curricular unit example and discuss design tensions in doing this work.

papers.title: Investigating the Influence of AI-Augmented Summarization on Concept Learning, Summarization Skills, Argumentative Essay Writing, and Course Outcomes in Online Adult Education
papers.authors: Jinho Kim, Yoojin Bae, Jonathan Stravelakis, Min Kyu Kim
papers.modelling_usage: **Learning Technologies & Modeling Environments**: Examines software environments, automated feedback systems, or digital scaffolding designed to facilitate iterative student modeling practices. Evidence: "This study aims to explore the influence of concept learning facilitated by an AI-augmented summarization feedback tool, the Student Mental Model Analyzer for Research and Teaching (SMART..."
papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the influence of concept learning facilitated by an AI-augmented summarization feedback tool, the Student Mental Model Analyzer for Research and Teaching (SMART), on various learning outcomes within an undergraduate English course using linear mixed-effects (LME) modeling and Bayesian correlations with data from 22 participants. Significant improvements in learners’ mental models and associations of concept learning with subsequent learning activities suggest the potential of such tools in improving learning performance.

papers.title: Estimating Action-Specific Expertise in AR-Guided Learning and Training by Modeling Visual Attention
papers.authors: Dong Woo Yoo, Hamid Tarashiyoun, Mohsen Moghaddam
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "The study contributes to the field of learning sciences by enhancing the effectiveness and personalization of AR learning and training models."
papers.abstract: This paper explores a new method for estimating expertise in Augmented Reality (AR) learning and training, emphasizing the learner’s familiarity with action-relevant Areas of Interest (AoI) and their decision-making processes. By examining both gaze behavior and object tracking based on egocentric video data from a group of 15 participants, we investigate the interaction dynamics of learners within AR environments to distinguish between expert and novice behaviors. Key findings highlight notable variations in visual attention and engagement strategies, reflecting different degrees of task familiarity and decision-making capabilities among participants with varying self-reported expertise levels. This approach advances the understanding of visual attention behavior and its relation with expertise in the context of AR learning, offering new insights for the design of adaptive, learner-centered AR education systems. The study contributes to the field of learning sciences by enhancing the effectiveness and personalization of AR learning and training models.

papers.title: Broadening Participation in STEM-based Computational Modeling by Leveraging Alternatives to Programming
papers.authors: Kevin W. McElhaney, Satabdi Basu, Nonye Alozie, Nicole Hutchins, Arif Rachmatullah, Kelly Mills, Gautam Biswas
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Computational models (CMs) offer pre-college students opportunities to integrate STEM disciplines with computational thinking in ways that reflect authentic STEM practice."
papers.abstract: Computational models (CMs) offer pre-college students opportunities to integrate STEM disciplines with computational thinking in ways that reflect authentic STEM practice. However, not all STEM teachers and students are prepared to teach or learn programming skills required to construct CMs. To broaden participation in computing, we propose instructional approaches that integrate STEM with CMs without requiring students to program, thereby alleviating challenges associated with learning how to program.

papers.title: Using Biterm Topic Modeling to Explore Gender Differences in Secondary Students’ Wonderings about AI Concepts
papers.authors: Doreen Mushi, Jie Chao, Shiyan Jiang, Rebecca Ellis, Carolyn P. Rosé, Kenia Wiedemann
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "The findings revealed that keywords related to model accuracy and prediction such as Words and Weights were prevalent in both groups."
papers.abstract: The study reveals gender-based differences in how secondary students express curiosity in an AI curriculum. The study used biterm topic modeling to explore questions posed by male and female learners (n=239) in Grades 8-12. The findings revealed that keywords related to model accuracy and prediction such as Words and Weights were prevalent in both groups. Key variations were observed in technical terms, such as Machines. The discussions highlight the need for socially relevant AI curriculums.

papers.title: Exploring the Affective Dimension of Integrating Computational Modeling with Science Learning
papers.authors: Jennifer Elisabeth Mesiner, Aditi Wagh
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "In this poster, we analyze video data of a pair of students’ computational modeling to illustrate the role that epistemic emotions of surprise and uncertainty played in them conducting th..."
papers.abstract: There is a movement in science education towards engaging students in authentic disciplinary practices, including computational modeling. This paper reports on a pilot study from a larger project in which we designed computational modeling curricula for public high school STEM classrooms. In this poster, we analyze video data of a pair of students’ computational modeling to illustrate the role that epistemic emotions of surprise and uncertainty played in them conducting their own investigations.

papers.title: The Process of Constructing Interdisciplinary Thinking Through Graduation Research in an Interdisciplinary Department
papers.authors: Go Shoji, Shigeto Ozawa
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Using Trajectory Equifinality Modeling (TEM), grounded in social constructivism, we conducted a qualitative analysis from the perspective of interdisciplinary thinking."
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate how students in an interdisciplinary department construct interdisciplinary thinking through their graduation research. Using Trajectory Equifinality Modeling (TEM), grounded in social constructivism, we conducted a qualitative analysis from the perspective of interdisciplinary thinking. The analysis revealed two types of processes in the construction of interdisciplinary thinking through graduation research. The first involves integrating a secondary field through external resources provided by supervisor, while the second entails developing interest in a secondary field due to the interdisciplinarity of seminars or supervisors. Students expanded their research themes by maintaining their primary field and incorporating insights from secondary fields. This study provides valuable insights for the development of interdisciplinary education designed to foster interdisciplinary thinking.

papers.title: A Multilevel Analysis of Factors Associated with Secondary School Teachers’ Perceived Digital Competence
papers.authors: Hulya Avci
papers.modelling_usage: **Statistical, Machine Learning & Quantitative Modeling**: Applies quantitative, statistical, or machine learning models (e.g., SEM, multilevel analysis, Markov, or network modeling) to examine learning processes and empirical outcomes. Evidence: "A two-level multilevel linear modeling was conducted to investigate the impact of (a) teachers' pre- and in-service ICT training, job satisfaction, and collegial collaboration in the teac..."
papers.abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between perceived digital competence and potential influencing factors among secondary school teachers. Data were drawn from the OECD’s Teaching and Learning International Survey 2018 U.S. national teacher survey of 165 schools and 2,414 secondary teachers. A two-level multilevel linear modeling was conducted to investigate the impact of (a) teachers' pre- and in-service ICT training, job satisfaction, and collegial collaboration in the teacher level and (b) collective teacher innovativeness, school innovativeness, and digital infrastructure in the school level. Results revealed several factors, including ICT training, collegial collaboration, and digital infrastructure, significantly predicted secondary teachers' perceived digital competence within and across schools. These findings are essential for understanding the multi-level aspects of digital competence and the potential for implementing interventions to fortify teacher training programs and promote collaborative efforts that can help cultivate a resilient and interconnected educational community.

papers.title: Turn Charts for Interaction Analysis: Visually Mapping the Conversation Floor
papers.authors: Benjamin R. Shapiro, Rogers Hall, Arpit Mathur, Edwin Zhao
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Findings highlight how turn charts extend current transcription techniques to (1) answer common questions in IA, (2) advance exploratory modeling in the early stages of IA, and (3) bridge..."
papers.abstract: In the Learning Sciences and CSCL communities, interaction analysis (IA) is an important methodological approach to studying teaching and learning. IA relies on transcripts to selectively encode, represent, and experience video. However, researchers using IA continue to highlight the need for more dynamic and interactive transcription techniques to interpret, experience, and even speculate about data in context. In this paper, we use a comparative case study to introduce a transcription technique we call turn charts. Turn charts integrate ideas in IA with interactive and alternative visualization to visually map conversation over time, while also providing dynamic ways to select and experience audio and video data. Findings highlight how turn charts extend current transcription techniques to (1) answer common questions in IA, (2) advance exploratory modeling in the early stages of IA, and (3) bridge IA and visualization research to expand how people, things, and context are represented.

papers.title: Students’ Prioritization of Initial and Direct Causal Mechanisms During Model Evaluation
papers.authors: Danielle Murphy, Ravit Golan Duncan, Clark A. Chinn, Joshua Danish, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Zachary Ryan, Jinzhi Zhou, Christina Stiso
papers.modelling_usage: **Scientific Inquiry & Explanatory Modeling**: Focuses on student practices of generating, testing, evaluating, and iteratively revising explanatory scientific models using empirical evidence. Evidence: "During a five-week model-based inquiry unit students identified causes of the phenomenon, eutrophication, but it was unclear whether student understood the causes hierarchically, i.e., wh..."
papers.abstract: Scientific modeling is supported by epistemic criteria to evaluate the “goodness” of scientific products. A central epistemic criterion is causal mechanism which means identifying the underlying causes which generate changes within a system. During a five-week model-based inquiry unit students identified causes of the phenomenon, eutrophication, but it was unclear whether student understood the causes hierarchically, i.e., whether some causes led to others, and whether some were more critical to include in a model than others. In a model evaluation task, students prioritized a model that was complete and had all the causes, deprioritized the model missing the direct causal mechanism, and placed models missing the initial causes in the middle. The results indicate that students thought about mechanisms in terms of chaining which means students thought about how causes led to outcomes within a system.

papers.title: Approaching “Filter Bubble” in Recommendation Systems: A Transformative AI Literacy Learning Experience
papers.authors: Yunfan Gong, Xiaofei Zhou, Yushan Zhou, April Luehmann, Yujung Han, Zhen Bai
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Transformative Experience model was integrated into learning activities design, focusing on making AI concepts relevant to students’ daily experiences, facilitating a new understanding of..."
papers.abstract: Young learners today are constantly influenced by AI recommendations, from media choices to social connections. The resulting "filter bubble" can limit their exposure to diverse perspectives, which is especially problematic when they are not aware this manipulation is happening or why. To address the need to support youth AI literacy, we developed "BeeTrap", a mobile Augmented Reality (AR) learning game designed to enlighten young learners about the mechanisms and the ethical issue of recommendation systems. Transformative Experience model was integrated into learning activities design, focusing on making AI concepts relevant to students’ daily experiences, facilitating a new understanding of their digital world, and modeling real-life applications. Our pilot study with middle schoolers in a community-based program primarily investigated how transformative structured AI learning activities affected students’ understanding of recommendation systems and their overall conceptual, emotional, and behavioral changes toward AI.

papers.title: Modeling with Primary Sources: An Approach to Teach Data Bias for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Education
papers.authors: Jeanne McClure, Juan Zheng, Franziska Bickel, Shiyan Jiang, Carolyn P. Rosé, Jie Chao, LaDale Winling
papers.modelling_usage: **Data & Comparative Modeling**: Investigates how learners build comparative models from large, unstructured, or socioeconomic datasets to construct evidence-based narratives. Evidence: "In this paper, we present the SourceML approach, teaching data bias by engaging students in building ML models with primary sources as text data in high school history classrooms."
papers.abstract: Data bias in AI (artificial intelligence) and ML (machine learning) remains a prominent challenge, with implications ranging from healthcare to criminal justice. As we lean more on these technologies, it becomes vital to educate the youth about the nuances of data bias and its implications. In this paper, we present the SourceML approach, teaching data bias by engaging students in building ML models with primary sources as text data in high school history classrooms. We have developed a web-based tool, StoryQ, designed to allow K-12 students to create ML models. Our results demonstrated that this approach enhances students’ understanding of data bias, helping them recognize diverse bias origins, societal implications, and comprehensive strategies for bias mitigation. The SourceML approach underscores the importance of fostering historical thinking in teaching data bias, highlighting the intricacies of data origin, generation context, and subtle influences shaping data.

papers.title: Modeling-Based Learning in Kindergarten Science: Investigating Heat Transfer in a Metal Rod
papers.authors: Loucas T. Louca, Melina Xeni
papers.modelling_usage: **Learning Technologies & Modeling Environments**: Examines software environments, automated feedback systems, or digital scaffolding designed to facilitate iterative student modeling practices. Evidence: "We use this evidence to argue that (a) different modeling tools may afford different learning opportunities; (b) kindergarten children have modeling resources that can use in order to uti..."
papers.abstract: Following research on using Modeling-based Learning (MbL) in kindergarten, in this interpretive case study we seek to provide detailed descriptions of the implementation of MbL with a group of 24 kindergarten children studying heat transfer in a metal rod. Focusing on children mechanistic reasoning and their constructed models, findings suggest that participating children successfully engaged in authentic MbL activities and developed several different types of models, utilizing a variety of features of mechanistic reasoning. We use this evidence to argue that (a) different modeling tools may afford different learning opportunities; (b) kindergarten children have modeling resources that can use in order to utilize different MbL tools; and (c) different MbL tools may prevent or support children moving into a lower scalar lever of a more advanced mechanistic account of the phenomenon.

papers.title: Fused Representations: Linking Choreographic and Digital NetLogo Modeling through Intermodal Inquiry
papers.authors: Aditi Wagh, Lauren Vogelstein, Dionne Champion
papers.modelling_usage: **Embodied & Participatory Modeling**: Leverages embodied, mixed-reality, or physical role-play activities to ground learners' sense-making and computational modeling of complex systems. Evidence: "Drawing on analysis of youth interviews, one group’s work towards preparing their final share-out, and their final share-out itself, we propose the construct of a fused representation—a d..."
papers.abstract: This paper reports from a summer camp, Dance to Explore Science, in which middle school youth, professional scientists and choreographers collaboratively engaged in intermodal inquiry using choreographic and digital NetLogo modeling to investigate a topic within the scientists’ research areas. Drawing on analysis of youth interviews, one group’s work towards preparing their final share-out, and their final share-out itself, we propose the construct of a fused representation—a distributed model developed by participants in which their physical choreography and NetLogo models expressed a scientific idea in interlinked ways. We present evidence of why we see their share-out as a fused representation, and illuminate how attuning to the relationships between their choreographic and NetLogo models led the group to construct a fused representation. In the discussion, we reflect on the importance of supporting the development of fused representations to leverage multiple modalities for scientific modeling and sense-making.

papers.title: Decomposing Students’ Design Moves when Programming Agent-Based Models
papers.authors: Adelmo Eloy, Tamar Fuhrmann, Aditi Wagh, Roseli de Deus Lopes, Michelle Wilkerson, Paulo Blikstein
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Using log data and video recordings from three pairs of students to find patterns in programming actions while interacting with an agent- and block-based modeling environment, we identify..."
papers.abstract: Constructing computational models is a central practice for K-12 students to refine and validate their understanding of scientific phenomena and develop computational practices. Our work decomposes that practice by investigating the design moves students take while constructing models through programming. Using log data and video recordings from three pairs of students to find patterns in programming actions while interacting with an agent- and block-based modeling environment, we identify six design moves students used. In addition, we situate the occurrence of those moves over time and provide vignettes that illustrate them in context. Finally, we reflect on how our findings support the argument that computational modeling, particularly programming models, provides a fertile ground for promoting modeling and computational practices.

papers.title: River Crossings of our Childhood: Nezuko and Yasmine Dis/orient Computing Education
papers.authors: Megha Sanyal, Pratim Sengupta, Pallavi Banerjee, Santanu Dutta, Basak Helvaci Ozacar
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "We present a case of two youth who are sisters and newcomer immigrants of color in Canada as they work towards re-designing and re-imagining computational models entrenched in white, colo..."
papers.abstract: We present a case of two youth who are sisters and newcomer immigrants of color in Canada as they work towards re-designing and re-imagining computational models entrenched in white, colonial, and masculine ideologies. Through their representational and epistemic work, we show how centering their desires, personal and sensory-affective histories can dis/orient colonial and techno-centric approaches to computational modeling. We also advance a varied range of scholarship that critiques the deficit positioning of newcomer immigrant and refugee youth of color by centring the youths’ proleptic world-making.

papers.title: Learning From Errors and Worked Examples to Address Common Misunderstandings in Linear Functions Knowledge
papers.authors: Noor Elagha, James Pellegrino
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Study 1 focused on identifying and modeling errors that students most commonly make during the essential conceptual and procedural components of the problem-solving process for different ..."
papers.abstract: A series of studies were conducted to explore designs for instructional interventions, including worked examples and learning from errors, that can address misunderstandings in linear functions (LF) knowledge of college students. Study 1 focused on identifying and modeling errors that students most commonly make during the essential conceptual and procedural components of the problem-solving process for different types of LF items. Study 2 then addressed common errors by testing the efficacy of different forms of worked example (WE) presentation. Findings from Study 2 led to changes in the design of the WE which were then tested in Study 3. Overall, the findings support the importance of tailoring learning interventions to the learner. Instructional interventions using WE and learning from errors can be tailored to address common misunderstandings for important mathematical topics such as LF.

papers.title: Investigating Melting And Freezing: How Different Scalar Levels Of Mechanistic Reasoning Look In Modeling-Based Learning In Kindergarten Science
papers.authors: Loucas Louca, Maro Michaelidou
papers.modelling_usage: **Data & Comparative Modeling**: Investigates how learners build comparative models from large, unstructured, or socioeconomic datasets to construct evidence-based narratives. Evidence: "Following research on using Modeling-based Learning (MbL) in kindergarten science education with an emphasis of mechanistic reasoning, this case study provides detailed descriptions of th..."
papers.abstract: Modeling has been recognized as a crucial element of science education. Following research on using Modeling-based Learning (MbL) in kindergarten science education with an emphasis of mechanistic reasoning, this case study provides detailed descriptions of the implementation of MbL with a group of 21 kindergarten children studying (a) ice cube melting and (b) water freezing. Data included transcribed lessons and child-developed models. We coded the discourse data for mechanistic reasoning, and child-constructed models using artifact analysis. Findings suggest that participating kindergarten children (a) can think productively across various scalar levels of mechanistic reasoning, although support to move across these levels is necessary; (b) working in a step-by-step process of progressive MbL is crucial for children before moving to lower scalar levels of reasoning; and (c) multiple ways of analyzing the data from children of these ages provide better insights into the MbL process.

papers.title: Artifactual Knowing in Collaborative Modeling Practices
papers.authors: Ayça K. Fackler, Laura A. Zangori, Mollie Botkin, Jamie N. Elsner, Troy D. Sadler
papers.modelling_usage: **Scientific Inquiry & Explanatory Modeling**: Focuses on student practices of generating, testing, evaluating, and iteratively revising explanatory scientific models using empirical evidence. Evidence: "In this exploratory case study, we analyzed how a group of middle school students positioned themselves, their peers, and the emerging modeling artifact during a collaborative modeling task."
papers.abstract: We use artifactual knowing and positioning theory as a lens to examine the development of a small group model. In this exploratory case study, we analyzed how a group of middle school students positioned themselves, their peers, and the emerging modeling artifact during a collaborative modeling task. We find that as the model emerged, it created a space where youth challenged assumptions, negotiated content, and redefined their positions through the artifact. Study implications suggest that how modeling artifacts emerge significantly shapes how modeling practices support student learning.

papers.title: Are We Still Teaching the Same Learning Sciences? A Ten-Year Follow-Up Analysis of Graduate Program Curricula
papers.authors: Melissa D. Oezsoy, Marvin Fendt, Meral Roeben, Katharina M. Bach, Marina Pfeifer, David Sachs, Daniel Sommerhoff, Freydis Vogel, Frank Fischer, Olga Chernikova
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Programs teaching non-parametric statistics, collaborative learning, and computational modeling showed the highest homogeneity."
papers.abstract: This study provides an updated overview of the concepts and methods in the Learning Sciences (LS) graduate programs, addressing the question posed by Sommerhoff et al. (2018) about what we teach in the LS. Analyzing 88 programs across institutions, we found a quantitative growth in programs. Most are concentrated in North America, with fewer in Europe and minimal representation in Australia and Asia. Key concepts include digital technology to support learning, learning in formal contexts, and the design of learning environments. Programs employ methods, including both quantitative and qualitative approaches, with design-based research and learning analytics being prevalent. Programs teaching non-parametric statistics, collaborative learning, and computational modeling showed the highest homogeneity. A decade later, we see that some former core concepts of LS have shifted to the periphery, while peripheral concepts, like diversity and equity, and methods are merging with the core, reflecting the LS as an innovative, dynamic community of practice.

papers.title: Taking a Scientist Perspective: Constructing Science Identities through Embodied Modeling
papers.authors: Selena Steinberg, Joshua Danish
papers.modelling_usage: **Embodied & Participatory Modeling**: Leverages embodied, mixed-reality, or physical role-play activities to ground learners' sense-making and computational modeling of complex systems. Evidence: "In embodied science modeling, perspective taking is often used to help students take on the different points of view within a scientific phenomenon to understand how it arises."
papers.abstract: In embodied science modeling, perspective taking is often used to help students take on the different points of view within a scientific phenomenon to understand how it arises. Perspective taking is also a central practice in identity construction (e.g. imagining and taking on new roles), yet the implications of perspective taking as scientific entities for students’ science identities is under explored. Therefore, we ask how fifth grade students construct science identities when they are taking on the perspective of a scientist in an embodied model versus acting as themselves. We draw on discursive psychology to conceptualize science identity, viewing it as the ways that students position themselves and are positioned by others in relation to science through discursive resources. We found that when students were acting as scientists, they positioned themselves and each other as scientific, but when they talked about their own scientific practices, they positioned themselves as non-scientific.

papers.title: Towards Expansive and Equitable Modeling: Syncretic Modeling through the Lenses of Dance, Science, and computation
papers.authors: Lauren Vogelstein, Aditi Wagh, Dionne Champion
papers.modelling_usage: **Embodied & Participatory Modeling**: Leverages embodied, mixed-reality, or physical role-play activities to ground learners' sense-making and computational modeling of complex systems. Evidence: "Using discourse, video stills, and narrative description of a group that modeled spinal cord injuries, we show how these three dimensions disrupted barriers between disciplines (science &..."
papers.abstract: Modeling is a cornerstone of professional scientific practice, however, there aren’t enough opportunities for youth to leverage their own perspectives when engaging in modeling inquiry. This paper describes three design dimensions—interdisciplinarity, intermodality, & intergenerationality--of a 2-week long summer camp that leveraged theories of syncretism to integrate dance, science and computing in order to support youth contributions in modeling practices. The camp engaged 12 middle school youth, 2 scientists and 3 choreographers in adopting a complex systems lens and engaging in collaborative inquiry around the scientists’ research systems using choreographic and digital NetLogo modeling. Using discourse, video stills, and narrative description of a group that modeled spinal cord injuries, we show how these three dimensions disrupted barriers between disciplines (science & dance), modes of sense-making (movement & computation), and inequitable power dynamics (youth and adults). In the discussion, we draw out contributions to the literature particularly on scientific modeling.

papers.title: Exploring AI-Generated Expert Models: Instructor Interaction and Learner Perceptions in a Physics Class
papers.authors: Golnoush Haddadian, Hyunkyu Han, Jinho Kim, Mohamed Shameer Abdeen, Min Kyu Kim
papers.modelling_usage: **Learning Technologies & Modeling Environments**: Examines software environments, automated feedback systems, or digital scaffolding designed to facilitate iterative student modeling practices. Evidence: "Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers opportunities for automatically creating expert model summaries, though creating them is demanding, requiring significant time and effort."
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers opportunities for automatically creating expert model summaries, though creating them is demanding, requiring significant time and effort. Using a case study, we explored three types of expert model summaries, generated by human, AI, and human-AI collaboration. A new, AI-augmented expert modeling tool, which supports summarization activities, was deployed. Human-AI interaction, linguistic differences among the summaries, and learners’ perceptions were explored. Data sources included instructor log data, linguistic measures, and a student evaluation survey. Results showed that students preferred AI-generated summaries for their clarity, depth, and coherence, while human-AI collaboration achieved a balance between fluency and accuracy. Findings signify GenAI’s potential to reduce workload but underscore the need to address its limitations.

papers.title: Exploring Out-of-Tutor Interventions by Teachers in Supporting Student Learning with AI Tutors
papers.authors: Shamya Karumbaiah, Anand Syamkumar
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Learning analytics has embraced the complexities of modeling student learning and engagement in ecological settings like K12 classrooms."
papers.abstract: Learning analytics has embraced the complexities of modeling student learning and engagement in ecological settings like K12 classrooms. While analyzing AI tutor interaction logs remains common, there is a growing need to include events that happen outside the AI tutor. Studies indicate teachers play active roles when students use AI tutors, and teacher support tools improve learning outcomes. However, methodological challenges exist in studying how such out-of-tutor interventions in the classroom shape learning (e.g., no counterfactual data, ethical issues in collecting control data). We propose a simple reconceptualization of the problem with which we could use standard statistical approaches to quantify the relationship between out-of-tutor interventions and student learning in the AI tutor. We study how moments of teacher help relate to improvements in students' performance on the skill or concept they were helped with. Our analysis reveals that teacher help has a significantly positive effect.

papers.title: Investigating Middle School Students’ Representations of Proportional Reasoning Understanding in a Challenge Based Learning Project through Making
papers.authors: Juan Torralba, Jorge Membrillo-Hernandez
papers.modelling_usage: **Mathematical & Digital Design Modeling**: Engages students in mathematical, probabilistic, or 3D digital design modeling to develop spatial and quantitative reasoning. Evidence: "Findings regarding the integration of professional technology and the prevalence of mathematical estimation in digital modeling provide avenues for further research vis-a-vis the role of ..."
papers.abstract: Proportional reasoning understanding is considered necessary for student success in upper-level mathematics as well as science, technology, and engineering. Research on middle grades mathematics learning shows that students tend to development stronger understandings of mathematical concepts when they learn through constructionist real-world projects that are relevant and meaningful to them. In this work, we conducted an exploratory qualitative study to investigate how middle school students demonstrate their understanding of proportional reasoning through making in a Challenge-Based Learning project. Our findings showed that students accurately represented their understanding of proportionality through their digital artifacts more than any other modality available, contrasting previous findings in the relevant literature. Findings regarding the integration of professional technology and the prevalence of mathematical estimation in digital modeling provide avenues for further research vis-a-vis the role of estimation in spatial reasoning for design. Implications for the practice and the field of STEM learning are discussed.

papers.title: Modeling the Knowledge Underlying Student Engagement in Theory-Building Practices
papers.authors: Hillary Swanson
papers.modelling_usage: **Scientific Inquiry & Explanatory Modeling**: Focuses on student practices of generating, testing, evaluating, and iteratively revising explanatory scientific models using empirical evidence. Evidence: "Grounded in the knowledge in pieces (KiP) perspective, the ESF is designed to produce high-precision models of the structure, dynamics, and development of the knowledge students use to co..."
papers.abstract: Science practices are a critical component of science education. Theory-building practices such as modeling lie at the heart of the scientific enterprise. To develop instructional activities that engage students in theory-building practices and assessments that track their development of expertise, it is necessary to understand the knowledge underlying students’ engagement in theory building. This paper presents a framework for modeling this knowledge, called the epistemic systems framework (ESF). Grounded in the knowledge in pieces (KiP) perspective, the ESF is designed to produce high-precision models of the structure, dynamics, and development of the knowledge students use to construct and refine theoretical artifacts, including models and explanations. The paper outlines the framework’s theoretical foundations and unpacks its major components.

papers.title: “Kind of Like a Chemical Reaction”: Leveraging Structural Similarities between Models to Support Teachers' Growing Expertise with Computational Modeling for Science Teaching
papers.authors: Daniel Wendel, Aditi Wagh, Jennifer Elisabeth Mesiner
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "In this paper, we illustrate how teachers working with a (serendipitous) analogy between a familiar process and a topic covered in chemistry class–frogs catching flies and reaction rates–..."
papers.abstract: There is consensus that computational modeling can support integration of science with computing for student learning. However, it can be challenging for teachers to gain comfort with this relatively new practice, reconcile how it relates to science, and recognize its pedagogical value. In this paper, we illustrate how teachers working with a (serendipitous) analogy between a familiar process and a topic covered in chemistry class–frogs catching flies and reaction rates–enabled them to take up computational modeling in their science teaching. Drawing on notes from co-design sessions, teacher interviews and student worksheets, we illustrate how a focal teacher shifted from initial reluctance to taking ownership of designing and teaching a computational modeling lesson sequence. We also briefly show how her students took up this work. Finally, we reflect on the importance of leveraging teachers’ existing domain and pedagogical expertise as we bring these new practices into their classrooms.

papers.title: Enhancing the Relevance of Science Learning: Exploring the Potential of the Student Experience Improvement Cycle
papers.authors: Ali Raza, William R. Penuel, Jiawei Li, Kenneth A. Frank
papers.modelling_usage: **Statistical, Machine Learning & Quantitative Modeling**: Applies quantitative, statistical, or machine learning models (e.g., SEM, multilevel analysis, Markov, or network modeling) to examine learning processes and empirical outcomes. Evidence: "Analyses from hierarchical linear modeling indicated students’ perceptions of relevance increased significantly over time and that Black/African American students’ perceptions of experien..."
papers.abstract: To support equitable instruction in science, the Framework envisions implementing science instruction around students’ interests and experiences. In this study, we tested a strategy for using student experience data for data-informed decision-making called the Student Experience Improvement Cycle (SEIC), which engages groups of educators and a coach in adapting evidence-based practices for enhancing the relevance of instruction to students and their communities. This study investigated the effects of the SEIC using a single-group, pretest-posttest design using experience-based exit ticket surveys collected from middle school science students. Analyses from hierarchical linear modeling indicated students’ perceptions of relevance increased significantly over time and that Black/African American students’ perceptions of experience increased more than a reference group of Latinx students.

papers.title: Towards InCoRe - An Interactive Co-Regulation Model for training Teacher Classroom Communication Skills
papers.authors: Chirag Bhuvaneshwara, Lara Chehayeb, Alexander Haberl, Julius Siedentopf, Patrick Gebhard, Dimitra Tsovaltzi
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "This short paper introduces InCoRe, a conceptual and early-stage implementation of an interactive co-regulation model aimed at supporting teacher training in classroom communication and s..."
papers.abstract: This short paper introduces InCoRe, a conceptual and early-stage implementation of an interactive co-regulation model aimed at supporting teacher training in classroom communication and socio-emotional conflict management. InCoRe is embedded within MITHOS, a hybrid AI training system combining psychodynamic theory and computational affect modeling to interpret teacher emotional experiences during classroom conflicts. Grounded in Operationalized Psychodynamic Diagnostics and conflict resolution theory, the model identifies internal conflicts, lead affects, and behavioral intentions to guide virtual student responses. We present findings from a Wizard-of-Oz study validating the mapping between subjective emotional experiences and conflict regulation styles. Results demonstrate the feasibility of InCoRe for real-time interpretation of co-regulation behavior, setting the stage for more comprehensive system deployment and large-scale validation.

papers.title: The Effects of Emotion Regulation and Students’ Perceived Challenges on Emotion Synchrony in Collaborative Learning
papers.authors: Xiaoshan Huang, Shan Li, Tingting Wang, Susanne P. Lajoie
papers.modelling_usage: **Statistical, Machine Learning & Quantitative Modeling**: Applies quantitative, statistical, or machine learning models (e.g., SEM, multilevel analysis, Markov, or network modeling) to examine learning processes and empirical outcomes. Evidence: "We performed the partial least squares structural equation modeling for data analysis."
papers.abstract: In this study, we explored the relationships among students’ perceived challenges in collaborative learning, emotion regulation strategies (i.e., reappraisal and suppression), and emotion synchrony (i.e., valence synchrony and arousal synchrony) in natural classroom settings. We performed the partial least squares structural equation modeling for data analysis. The results revealed a positive and direct effect of cognitive reappraisal on arousal synchrony, and a negative and direct effect of cognitive reappraisal on valence synchrony. Students’ perceived challenges had a negative effect on their arousal synchrony. Students’ perceived challenges also played a mediating role in the relationship between cognitive reappraisal and arousal synchrony. As a total effect, cognitive reappraisal still positively and significantly predicted arousal synchrony. This study provided insights into students’ emotional responses in collaborative learning and informed the design of collaborative learning environments. This study has also methodological implications regarding the analysis of emotion synchrony.

papers.title: A Latent Growth Modeling for Individual Differences in Dispositions Toward Uncertainty Navigation in Computing Problem-solving
papers.authors: Jongchan Park, Ying-Chih Chen, Yuli Deng, Garima Agrawal, Huan Liu
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "A latent growth model was tested to examine inter- and intra-individual differences in DUNC and the impact of achievement goals (mastery and performance) and gender."
papers.abstract: In authentic problem-solving, students may exhibit various patterns of uncertainty navigation, reflecting their dispositions toward uncertainty navigation in computing problem-solving (DUNC). This study investigates how DUNC evolves—advancing, maintaining, or retreating— over time across multiple problem-solving learning sessions. A latent growth model was tested to examine inter- and intra-individual differences in DUNC and the impact of achievement goals (mastery and performance) and gender. Data collected from 431 Fall 2023 cloud-computing students was used. Results revealed variability in DUNC trajectories: some students showed increases, decreases, or stability over time. Higher mastery goals were associated with higher initial DUNC and faster changes, while higher performance goals correlated with lower initial DUNC and slower changes. Gender did not significantly predict DUNC changes. The findings highlight that authentic problem-solving sessions can enhance DUNC and that fostering mastery goal orientations may accelerate its development, reinforcing the value of DUNC in preparing future computer scientists.

papers.title: Computational Thinking Without Writing Code: What’s Next for Computational Modeling?
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Gabrielle Rabinowitz, Amanda Peel, Sharin Jacob, Quinn Burke, Ari Krakowski, Eric Greenwald, Preeti Gupta, Rachel Chaffee, Emma Anderson, Kirsten Peterson, Joyce Malyn-Smith, Beatriz Perret, John Chen, Uri Wilensky, Daniel Wendel, Aileen Han, Aditi Wagh, Paulo Blikstein, Michelle H. Wilkerson, Kate Moore, Helen Zhang, Mark Weckel, Ahmad Shah, Ji Hye Park, Safinah Ali, Alex Perez, Shuchi Grover, Irene Lee
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "The ten posters in this symposium provide different perspectives on the changing landscape and present examples of educational programs, professional development strategies, pedagogical a..."
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces exciting new possibilities and challenges to the established field of computational modeling education. The ten posters in this symposium provide different perspectives on the changing landscape and present examples of educational programs, professional development strategies, pedagogical approaches, and digital tools that have helped learners and educators develop the skills needed to interrogate and co-create scientific computational models with AI. The posters address each stage of computational modeling education, including reading and decoding models, modifying existing models, creating (or co-creating) models, and evaluating models.

papers.title: Exploring Hidden Affordances of Modeling Infrastructures for Epistemic Agency
papers.authors: Ashlyn Pierson, Kathryn Lanouette, Corey Brady
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "To address this tension, we present a case of a student’s work with a computational model."
papers.abstract: In science curricula, there are tensions between providing access to disciplinary practices and empowering students’ epistemic agency. To address this tension, we present a case of a student’s work with a computational model. The student’s creative and intuitive work deviated from the trajectory intended by the curriculum. By illustrating how the student’s resistance to classroom activities produced meaningful learning, our analysis will challenge what researchers and educators might consider “on task” or “productive” engagement.

papers.title: Do Gamers Learn Better From Games? – Insights From Hierarchical Linear Modelling
papers.authors: Chaewon Kim, Qian Zhang
papers.modelling_usage: **Statistical, Machine Learning & Quantitative Modeling**: Applies quantitative, statistical, or machine learning models (e.g., SEM, multilevel analysis, Markov, or network modeling) to examine learning processes and empirical outcomes. Evidence: "Using hierarchical linear modeling, the study found that gaming experience was the strongest predictor of learning outcomes, though marginally significant, while prior knowledge showed th..."
papers.abstract: This study examines how learner characteristics, including gaming experience, prior knowledge, and gender, influence learning gains in game-based learning. Using hierarchical linear modeling, the study found that gaming experience was the strongest predictor of learning outcomes, though marginally significant, while prior knowledge showed the greatest per-unit increase. Gender did not significantly affect outcomes, contradicting some previous findings. These results highlight the nuanced relationship between individual factors and game-based learning, emphasizing the importance of game type and instructional context.

papers.title: “I was debating and now I’m on board”: Supporting Shifts in Teacher Uptake of Computational Modeling in Science Classrooms
papers.authors: Aditi Wagh, Jennifer Elisabeth Mesiner, Daniel Wendel
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "This poster presents code-the-familiar modeling to foster teacher uptake of computational modeling using code."
papers.abstract: There is a need to examine how to support teacher uptake of computational modeling in science classrooms. This poster presents code-the-familiar modeling to foster teacher uptake of computational modeling using code. Drawing on a case study of two high school teachers from a research-practice partnership, we examine data from professional development and interviews to illustrate how teachers shift in their uptake, and share two lessons learned: Supporting bite-sized changes and leaning into teachers’ conceptual expertise.

papers.title: Pedagogical Responsibility in the Age of AI: Preservice Teachers’ Reasoning About Automated Scoring Technologies
papers.authors: Jessica Watkins
papers.modelling_usage: **Scientific Inquiry & Explanatory Modeling**: Focuses on student practices of generating, testing, evaluating, and iteratively revising explanatory scientific models using empirical evidence. Evidence: "Within a teacher education course on science modeling, students discussed current literature on machine learning methods for assessment."
papers.abstract: The use of AI for automated scoring of student work has been positioned as both transformative for and damaging to ambitious and equitable teaching. Yet throughout these debates, teachers’ voices have been noticeably absent. This paper considers how preservice teachers reason about the use of AI for assessing students’ science models. Within a teacher education course on science modeling, students discussed current literature on machine learning methods for assessment. Drawing on discourse analysis, I highlight how students made sense of the ideological, axiological, epistemological, and ontological dimensions of their role as future educators alongside their meaning making about the use of AI. The students alternately position AI as a “useful tool” for, “replica” of, or “unproductive barrier” to teachers’ work. With this analysis, I argue that supporting teacher learning about these technologies should involve helping them develop their pedagogical judgment about not just how, but whether these tools should be used.

papers.title: A Theoretical Proposal for Employing Temporal Hypergraphs to Model and Analyze Many-Body Interactions in Learning Processes
papers.authors: Koichi Yasutake, Hitoshi Inoue, Takahiro Tagawa
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Current analytical network models in Learning Sciences, grounded in classical graph theory, are inherently restricted to modeling pairwise relationships in learning."
papers.abstract: Learning is a dynamic and social process involving various relationships that unfold over time. Current analytical network models in Learning Sciences, grounded in classical graph theory, are inherently restricted to modeling pairwise relationships in learning. This study proposes the use of temporal hypergraph approach to Learning Sciences, a framework that enables the dynamic analysis of many-body interactions in learning contexts.

papers.title: Preservice Teachers’ Engagement with Systems Dynamic, Block-Based, and Paper-Pencil Models
papers.authors: Emanuel Eidin, Tamar Fuhrmann
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Data from screencasts and questionnaires revealed challenges in using computational tools to represent scientific concepts and suggested that static paper-pencil models may limit scaffold..."
papers.abstract: This pilot study explores how preservice teachers engage with paper-pencil, systems dynamic, and block-based computational models during a two-week science methods course. Despite recognizing the benefits of computational modeling, participants preferred paper-pencil models for future teaching. Data from screencasts and questionnaires revealed challenges in using computational tools to represent scientific concepts and suggested that static paper-pencil models may limit scaffolding for systems modeling. Findings highlight the need for scalable professional development in diverse modeling practices.

papers.title: Adapting the Use-Decode-Modify-Create Framework for Teacher Professional Learning about STEM-based Computational Activities
papers.authors: Kevin W. McElhaney, Hui Yang, Shruti Jain, Satabdi Basu
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "We describe the design of teacher professional learning activities based on the Use-Modify-Create instructional framework and examine how they prepared teachers to enact computational mod..."
papers.abstract: To effectively facilitate integrated STEM and computing instruction, K-12 teachers must support students’ engagement in computational practices. We describe the design of teacher professional learning activities based on the Use-Modify-Create instructional framework and examine how they prepared teachers to enact computational modeling activities. In interviews, teachers indicated that exploring simulations and evaluating code were helpful scaffolds for learning to construct computational models. Teachers also identified the need for additional supports for code interpretation and evaluation.

papers.title: Fostering AI Literacy through Opening the Black Box of Foundational Text Generation Models
papers.authors: Daria Smyslova, Franziska Bickel, Qiuqing Li, Shiyan Jiang, Rebecca Ellis, Jie Chao
papers.modelling_usage: **AI & Foundation Models**: Investigates foundational text generation and large language model architectures to examine AI literacy, model transparency, and learner interactions. Evidence: "This pilot study investigates the impact of an intervention aimed at demystifying foundational text generation models to enhance AI literacy among ninth-grade English Language Arts students."
papers.abstract: This pilot study investigates the impact of an intervention aimed at demystifying foundational text generation models to enhance AI literacy among ninth-grade English Language Arts students. Pre- and post-surveys revealed significant gains in self-assessed performance, while qualitative analysis showed improved understanding of concepts like predictive modeling. However, students struggled to connect foundational knowledge to advanced AI systems like ChatGPT. The findings highlight the importance of teaching foundational models and developing strategies to bridge this gap, supporting comprehensive AI literacy in K-12 education.

papers.title: Anchoring Code in Phenomena: Approaches to Integrating Domain-General Agent-based Modeling for Scientific Sensemaking into High School Classrooms
papers.authors: Emma Anderson, Daniel Wendel, Ilana Schoenfeld, Aditi Wagh
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Across the approaches, students use domain-general modeling to attend to structural and conceptual similarities and differences across phenomena and models, and extend their model/s to ex..."
papers.abstract: Drawing on co-design work with teachers, this poster presents four approaches to developing units that bring domain-general agent-based modeling into high school science classrooms. In each unit, scientific phenomena contextualize and support sense-making of code while students engage with code to make sense of phenomena. Across the approaches, students use domain-general modeling to attend to structural and conceptual similarities and differences across phenomena and models, and extend their model/s to explore key scientific ideas.

papers.title: Global Approaches to AIED: Common Voices and Silences about the Sustainable Use of Generative AI in Education
papers.authors: Hyo-Jeong So, Lynde Tan, Beaumie Kim
papers.modelling_usage: **AI & Foundation Models**: Investigates foundational text generation and large language model architectures to examine AI literacy, model transparency, and learner interactions. Evidence: "Our study conducted a thematic analysis through topic modeling to investigate global guidelines for GenAI use and explored critical considerations for educators, policymakers, and researc..."
papers.abstract: International organizations (e.g., UNESCO, UNICEF, and OECD) have published recommendations for generative AI (GenAI) in education, addressing pedagogical, ethical, and safety concerns. Our study conducted a thematic analysis through topic modeling to investigate global guidelines for GenAI use and explored critical considerations for educators, policymakers, and researchers. We aim to present common voices, and amplify silences about GenAI in education and discuss the ethical and moral implications of its sustainable uses.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: Student Motivations in an Unpackable-Block-Based Computational Modeling Environment
papers.authors: Adelmo Eloy, Tamar Fuhrmann, Roseli de Deus Lopes, Paulo Blikstein, Aditi Wagh
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "We found that unpacking and modifying blocks supported students in both exploring scientific ideas and addressing specific goals of computational modeling, providing insights on how unpac..."
papers.abstract: Engaging with computational models is central to both scientific and computational learning. A promising approach to “lower the floor” and make computational modeling more accessible is the development of domain-specific and block-based environments, which reduce programming complexity while leveraging students’ intuitions about scientific ideas. To balance usability and expressiveness in these environments, we develop the feature of “unpacking” blocks, allowing users to open and modify high-level blocks into the simpler constituent elements that define them. In this study, we analyze high school students’ models, screen recordings, and artifact-based interviews to investigate their motivation for modifying domain-specific blocks for eutrophication in aquatic ecosystems. We found that unpacking and modifying blocks supported students in both exploring scientific ideas and addressing specific goals of computational modeling, providing insights on how unpacking domain-specific blocks can support both computing and science learning.

papers.title: Rethinking Cognitive Apprenticeship Through Studio Pedagogy
papers.authors: Edith Bouton, Adam Lefstein, Zvi Bekerman, Sarah Michaels
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Second, modeling in studios occurs reactively and fragmentally within students' work process, contrary to the theory's prescribed proactive, comprehensive, performative demonstrations."
papers.abstract: This poster critically examines cognitive apprenticeship theory through systematic analysis of studio pedagogy in practice. Both pedagogies are rooted in traditional apprenticeship practices. Drawing on a semester-long observational study of a ceramics design studio in leading arts academy in Israel, we analyze interactional episodes to identify fundamental differences between the cognitive apprenticeship theoretical prescriptions and actual studio practices. We found that studio pedagogy manages to achieve many stated goals of cognitive apprenticeship, within educational and academic settings, while successfully maintaining the challenges that many cognitive apprenticeship implementation efforts face. There are several fundamental misalignments between cognitive apprenticeship theory and studio practices. First, studios shifts the traditional master-apprentice power dynamic, with instructors supporting students' visions rather than imposing their own. Second, modeling in studios occurs reactively and fragmentally within students' work process, contrary to the theory's prescribed proactive, comprehensive, performative demonstrations. Third, studio instructional support intensifies with project complexity, challenging the theory's fading support model. While studio pedagogy and cognitive apprenticeship in k12 settings are inherently different, learning from successful studio settings can enrich our understanding of apprenticeship-based learning in educational and academic settings.

papers.title: Designing for Discourse: Enacting Responsive Teaching through Code Reflections in a Computational Modeling Unit
papers.authors: Aditi Wagh, Leah F. Rosenbaum, Adelmo Eloy, Tamar Fuhrmann, Brendan Henrique, Paulo Blikstein, Michelle H. Wilkerson
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "We reflect on how this progression was driven by shifts in the teachers’ comfort with code and computational modeling and the resources designers can offer to educators to support the dev..."
papers.abstract: An emerging body of work in the learning sciences has examined how computational models can support teachers in responding to students' prompts, inquiry, and ideas. This work has highlighted how teachers make discursive moves in relation to computational models to support classroom discussion. In this paper, we focus on a complementary phenomenon: teachers' design of code reflections, or curricular modifications that deepen students' engagement with one another's code for scientific and computational sensemaking. We highlight how these code reflections advanced student discourse and how both the code reflections and discourse became more sophisticated over time, shifting towards making connections across code, behaviors, simulation outcomes, data and the scientific process being represented. We reflect on how this progression was driven by shifts in the teachers’ comfort with code and computational modeling and the resources designers can offer to educators to support the development of code reflections.

papers.title: Unplugged Activities as Opportunities to Enhance Mixed Reality Educational Technology through Personal Connections
papers.authors: Efrat Ayalon, Alicia C. Lane, Gabriella Anton, Tessaly Jen, Sarah Jaewon Lee, Noel Enyedy
papers.modelling_usage: **Embodied & Participatory Modeling**: Leverages embodied, mixed-reality, or physical role-play activities to ground learners' sense-making and computational modeling of complex systems. Evidence: "Through storytelling and design activities, students integrated personal experiences—such as caring for pets—into the modeling process, shaping how they modified the MR environment and re..."
papers.abstract: This paper explores how unplugged activities can enhance learning in mixed-reality (MR) science environments by supporting students in connecting classroom modeling with their lived experiences. Drawing on funds of knowledge (FoK) and embodied modeling learning theories, we analyze a case study of fourth-grade students engaged in a multi-modal ecosystem simulation. Through storytelling and design activities, students integrated personal experiences—such as caring for pets—into the modeling process, shaping how they modified the MR environment and reasoned about ecological systems. We find that unplugged activities can boost engagement by “doubling down” on the immersive, affective strengths of MR or counterbalance its limitations by rooting inquiry in students’ everyday knowledge. However, we also identify tensions when students’ emotional attachments to modeled agents override broader system-level reasoning. This work highlights the importance of designing unplugged activities as intentional mediational tools in socio-technical learning systems.

papers.title: Intertwining Epistemic and Relational Work in Scientific Modeling
papers.authors: Eve Manz, Annabel Stoler
papers.modelling_usage: **Scientific Inquiry & Explanatory Modeling**: Focuses on student practices of generating, testing, evaluating, and iteratively revising explanatory scientific models using empirical evidence. Evidence: "As youth and teachers engage in modeling conversations, they are simultaneously negotiating how knowledge is generated and how people are accountable to each other in a community."
papers.abstract: As youth and teachers engage in modeling conversations, they are simultaneously negotiating how knowledge is generated and how people are accountable to each other in a community. Typically, design and analysis have privileged the epistemic focus, including within a recent emphasis on sensemaking and collective knowledge development. In this paper, we examine epistemic and relational work during science classroom modeling conversations. We share a close analysis of a typical conversation structure, where individuals present models and other students evaluate and build from their ideas. We show how classroom members experienced relational challenges and opportunities in these conversations. We also examine how alternative structures taken up by teachers and students presented different opportunities and constraints. This work contributes to the field’s understanding of science practices and suggests implications for work on evaluation and care in science classrooms.

papers.title: Emotional Dynamics in Asynchronous Math Discussions: Analyzing the Impact of Negative Emotions on Learning Outcomes
papers.authors: Taehyun Kim, Zifeng Liu, Wanli Xing, Hai Li, Hyunju Oh
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Topic modeling and sequential pattern mining show that students with low negative emotions engage more productively, focusing on both 'Help-seeking behaviors' and 'Understanding.' In cont..."
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of negative emotions in asynchronous online math discussions and their impact on learning. Using data from 402 students and 3,084 discussion posts, the study employs sentiment analysis and machine learning to categorize emotions. Findings reveal that low levels of negative emotions can enhance learning by fostering active engagement, while higher levels correlate with lower performance. Topic modeling and sequential pattern mining show that students with low negative emotions engage more productively, focusing on both 'Help-seeking behaviors' and 'Understanding.' In contrast, high negative emotions lead to shorter interactions and focusing primarily on 'Help-seeking behaviors.' Sequential analysis indicates that low negative emotions often transition to neutral or positive states, supporting continued engagement, while high negative emotions result in repetitive negative sequences and disengagement. These findings underscore the importance of understanding negative emotions and providing appropriate support in asynchronous learning environments to foster engagement and improve outcomes.

papers.title: Podcasts as Public Pedagogy: Diagnostic and Prognostic Framing as Processes of Ideological Articulation in the Politics of Women’s Sports
papers.authors: Tanner Vea, Molly V. Shea
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "We combine recent learning sciences theorizations of ideology as interactional sensemaking with conceptualizations of diagnostic and prognostic framing from social movement studies to sho..."
papers.abstract: Podcasts have taken a prominent role in the construction of sociopolitical reality. In this paper, we use critical discourse analysis with a focus on discourses of victimhood to analyze two podcast episodes about women’s sports, “The Fundamental Rule of the W: No Place for -isms” from the podcast A Touch More and “A Stolen Dream” from The Joyful Warriors Podcast. We combine recent learning sciences theorizations of ideology as interactional sensemaking with conceptualizations of diagnostic and prognostic framing from social movement studies to show how podcast participants construct divergent visions of social problems in women’s sports and their solutions, modeling sociopolitical sensemaking as a form of public pedagogy. Broader social concerns about race and gender both become problems for women’s sports and echo out into a more encompassing sociopolitical landscape, with implications for collective sensemaking that will shape who belongs in society.

papers.title: The Role of Science Proficiency in Students’ Engagement with Computational Modeling Practices
papers.authors: Satabdi Basu, Arif Rachmatullah, Shruti Jain, Keun-Woo Lee, Kevin W. McElhaney
papers.modelling_usage: **Computational & Agent-Based Modeling**: Engages students in constructing, programming, or debugging computational and agent-based simulation models to explore dynamic scientific or social phenomena. Evidence: "Students participated in an integrated Science, Engineering, and Computational Modeling unit through one of three distinct instructional versions: Construct a CM, Interpret-and-Evaluate a..."
papers.abstract: Computational modeling of scientific systems is a powerful approach for fostering science and computational thinking (CT) proficiencies. However, the role of programming activities for this synergistic learning remains unclear. This paper examines alternative ways to engage with computational models (CM) beyond programming. Students participated in an integrated Science, Engineering, and Computational Modeling unit through one of three distinct instructional versions: Construct a CM, Interpret-and-Evaluate a CM, and Explore-and-Evaluate a simulation. Analyzing 188 student responses to a science+CT embedded assessment task, we investigate how science proficiency and instructional versions related to pseudocode interpretation and debugging performances. We found that students in the Explore-and-Evaluate a simulation outperformed students in the programming-based versions on the CT assessment items. Additionally, science proficiency strongly predicted students’ CT performance, unlike prior programming experience. These results highlight the promise of diverse approaches for fostering CT practices with implications for STEM+C instruction and assessment design.

papers.title: Learning from Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design
papers.authors: Shulong Yan, Yu Xia
papers.modelling_usage: **Conceptual & Theoretical Modeling**: Proposes or applies a conceptual framework or theoretical model to structure understanding of learning mechanisms, collaboration, or disciplinary practices. Evidence: "Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses."
papers.abstract: This study investigates how learning from failure can be supported through game design feedback activities in a virtual collaborative environment. Through analyzing video recordings of three checkpoint sessions in a two-week virtual game design camp with nine youth participants (ages 8-13), we identified six feedback styles and examined how designers responded to feedback. Our findings reveal that game design feedback in virtual environments transcends traditional linear relationships, forming a complex discursive relationship among testers, designers, and game artifacts. Screen sharing emerged as a crucial boundary object, facilitating communication and transforming traditional critique sessions into collaborative learning experiences. Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses. The study demonstrates that successful virtual design feedback requires thoughtfully curated environments that balance structured facilitation with playful engagement. These findings have implications for design education in virtual settings and suggest new approaches for supporting learning from failure in collaborative contexts.

papers.title: Friendly Controversy: Synergistic Scaffolding for Practices of Providing Peer Critique
papers.authors: Jinzhi Zhou, Qiuyu Lin, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Joshua Danish, Ravit Golan Duncan, Clark A. Chinn, Aman Desai
papers.modelling_usage: **Learning Technologies & Modeling Environments**: Examines software environments, automated feedback systems, or digital scaffolding designed to facilitate iterative student modeling practices. Evidence: "Drawing on distributed and synergistic scaffolding, we designed multiple supports within a CSCL modeling environment, including integrated evidence and peer-feedback mechanisms, to help 6..."
papers.abstract: Peer critique is essential for collaborative learning of science but presents challenges for students. Drawing on distributed and synergistic scaffolding, we designed multiple supports within a CSCL modeling environment, including integrated evidence and peer-feedback mechanisms, to help 6th-grade students develop peer critique practices. Through analysis of students’ comments and engagement patterns during critique activities, we found that students demonstrated progressive uptake of peer critique practices that the scaffolds were designed to promote, evident in more balanced, specific critiques over time. These findings inform the design of distributed scaffolds for supporting peer critique in science classrooms.
